t: None of the funds provided in this Act under “U.S. Customs and Border Protection—Operations and Support” for facilities shall be available until U.S. Customs and Border Protection establishes policies (via directive, procedures, guidance, and/or memorandum) and training programs to ensure that such facilities adhere to the National Standards on Transport, Escort, Detention, and Search, published in October of 2015:  Provided, That not later than 90 days after the date of enactment of this Act, U.S. Customs and Border Protection shall provide a detailed report to the Committees on Appropriations of the Senate and the House of Representatives, the Committee on the Judiciary of the Senate, and the House Judiciary Committee regarding the establishment and implementation of such policies and training programs.

fable.w: The tempting reading is that the required policies and the detailed report amount to a participatory process. The policies are set internally by directive, procedures, guidance or memorandum, not by rulemaking with public comment. The report goes only to congressional committees, which are inside the federal government. No state, tribe, expert, company or member of the public is consulted or given a right to object or sue.
fable.s: U.S. Customs and Border Protection shall provide a detailed report to the Committees on Appropriations of the Senate and the House of Representatives

opus.w: The only formal interaction here is a report to congressional committees, and Congress is inside the federal government. CBP's policies are set through internal directives, procedures, guidance or memoranda, not through rulemaking or any process that brings in outside parties. No one outside the federal government is consulted or given a role in the decision, so this is not participation.
opus.s: U.S. Customs and Border Protection shall provide a detailed report to the Committees on Appropriations of the Senate and the House of Representatives, the Committee on the Judiciary of the Senate, and the House Judiciary Committee
opus.b: 1. **Analysis.** Two readings could tempt a "Yes." The first is that CBP must "establish policies" before the funds become available, which looks a bit like rulemaking. But the section says the policies come "via directive, procedures, guidance, and/or memorandum." Those are internal agency tools. Nothing requires regulations, a comment period or any outside input. The second is the "detailed report" requirement. That report goes only to congressional committees, which are inside the federal government. No state, expert, company or member of the public takes part in any decision.

qwen_chat.w: The section requires U.S. Customs and Border Protection to establish internal policies and submit a report to Congressional committees. Congress is part of the federal government, so reporting to it is intra-governmental communication, not participation with outside parties. There is no requirement to consult with states, tribes, the public, or other non-federal entities.
qwen_chat.s: U.S. Customs and Border Protection shall provide a detailed report to the Committees on Appropriations of the Senate and the House of Representatives, the Committee on the Judiciary of the Senate, and the House Judiciary Committee regarding the establishment and implementation of such policies and training programs.
qwen_chat.b: Tempting-but-wrong reading: One might argue that the requirement to establish policies and training programs implies a need for consultation with outside experts or stakeholders to ensure the policies are effective. However, the text itself does not mandate any such consultation; it only mandates the creation of the policies and the submission of a report. Furthermore, the report is sent to Congressional committees, which are inside the federal government.
